context: Black Sea total surface area 422000 km²; semi-enclosed basin connected to Mediterranean via Turkish Straits (Bosphorus + Sea of Marmara + Dardanelles); receives freshwater from Dnieper Danube Dniester Don rivers; major rivers drain Chernobyl-contaminated catchments
notes: Drainage basin area ~2.4 million km²; ~25% of Black Sea drainage basin received measurable Chernobyl fallout; major rivers (Dnieper Danube Dniester) all contaminated by Chernobyl fallout

context: Permanent halocline (pycnocline) at 100-150m depth divides: oxic surface layer (oxygenated; biologically productive) from anoxic deep water (H2S-rich; permanently stratified); radionuclides deposited at surface are effectively confined to upper 100-150m
notes: The permanent stratification means Chernobyl radionuclides deposited in 1986 CANNOT be mixed into the 2100m deep anoxic layer by wind-driven mixing; residence time of surface water ~200-300 years before exiting through Bosphorus; unique oceanographic feature confines contamination to surface
source: Murray JW et al. 1989 Deep Sea Res; Mirzoyeva 2013; dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv

context: Direct atmospheric deposition of Cs-137 onto Black Sea surface during Chernobyl plume passage; estimated 300-500 Bq/m² average over Black Sea; total ~130-200 TBq Cs-137 direct fallout on Black Sea surface; Northwestern areas received higher deposition (500-1500 Bq/m²)
notes: Direct fallout on sea was comparable to river input for Cs-137; however Cs-137 is particle-reactive and adsorbs to sediments quickly; settling in anoxic bottom prevents remobilization; Black Sea sediments now serve as long-term Cs-137 sink
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; Bossew 2004 Sci Total Environ; Buesseler KO 1987 Nature

context: Peak Cs-137 in Black Sea surface water 1987 (combining fallout + initial river input); highest in NW Black Sea near Dnieper mouth; declined to 100-200 Bq/m³ by 1990
notes: For context: WHO drinking water limit for Cs-137 is 10,000 Bq/m³ (10 Bq/L); Black Sea peak was 200-400 Bq/m³ = well below limit; not a direct health risk; ecological and monitoring significance
source: Povinec PP et al. 2004 Sci Mar; UNSCEAR 2008; Stokozov NA et al.

context: Current Cs-137 = 56 Bq/m³ = 0.056 Bq/L; well below WHO limit (10 Bq/L = 10,000 Bq/m³); still elevated above pre-Chernobyl weapons testing background of ~2-5 Bq/m³ (pre-1986 nuclear tests contributed ~150-250 Bq/m³ in 1960s peak)
notes: Chernobyl Cs-137 superimposed on declining nuclear test baseline; decline from Chernobyl peak follows: physical decay (30yr half-life); dilution; sediment scavenging; export through Bosphorus; current level will continue declining toward background over next 50-100 years
source: dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv; J Environ Radioact Black Sea monitoring; Povinec 2004

context: Current Sr-90 = 32 Bq/m³ = 0.032 Bq/L; well below WHO guideline (10 Bq/L); primarily from weapons testing fallout globally (622 PBq Sr-90 from testing); Chernobyl contributed ~5-10% of current Black Sea Sr-90
notes: Global nuclear test Sr-90 dominates over Chernobyl contribution (622 PBq testing >> 10 PBq Chernobyl total); Chernobyl Sr-90 contribution ~5% after dilution in Black Sea; distinction from test Sr-90 requires isotopic analysis

context: Total Sr-90 delivered to Black Sea from Chernobyl-contaminated catchments via rivers 1986-2000: ~160 ± 28 TBq; split Dnieper ~100 TBq (63%); Danube ~60 TBq (37%); Danube catchment includes Austria Germany Czech Slovakia with significant Chernobyl deposition
notes: Sr-90 stays dissolved; river transport is primary Sr-90 delivery mechanism to Black Sea; contrast with Cs-137 where particle-reactive behavior traps >50% in Kyiv reservoir sediments (only 1-5% reaches Black Sea); see dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv

context: Cs-137 in Black Sea shelf sediments (0-200m depth); NW shelf near Dnieper mouth highest; organic-rich shelf sediments accumulate particle-reactive Cs-137; activity decreasing slowly (physical decay + burial by clean sediment)
notes: Sediment inventories integrate both direct fallout and river input; can be used to reconstruct annual deposition rates; Black Sea sediment core archive useful for tracing flood events and increased river input over decades
source: Gulin SB et al. J Environ Radioact 2008; Povinec 2004; IAEA Marine Environment Laboratory Monaco

context: Cs-137 export from Black Sea to Sea of Marmara and Mediterranean via Bosphorus surface current: estimated 2-5 TBq/yr in late 1980s; declining as Black Sea concentrations fell; total export 1986-2000 ~15-25 TBq Cs-137 to Mediterranean
notes: Bosphorus carries ~600 km³/yr of Black Sea surface water to Mediterranean; radionuclides in Black Sea are slowly exported; this is the dilution/loss mechanism for Black Sea contamination on decadal timescales
source: Guegueniat P 1994 J Environ Radioact; IAEA 2005 Marine radioactivity atlas

context: Cs-137 in Black Sea commercial fish (sprat anchovy mackerel): peaked 1987-1989; mostly <100 Bq/kg; well below EU limit 600 Bq/kg for fish (Regulation 2016/52); no closure of Black Sea fisheries required unlike Baltic and Scandinavian inland lakes
notes: Marine fish accumulate Cs-137 less efficiently than freshwater fish (seawater high in stable Cs competitive inhibition); Black Sea never required fisheries restrictions; contrast with Baltic: herring up to 400-500 Bq/kg in late 1980s
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; EU Commission food safety reports; food_agricultural_contamination_REAL.csv

context: Mytilus galloprovincialis (Black Sea mussel) Cs-137: 30-200 Bq/kg in 1987-1990 near Ukraine and Romania coasts; below commercial limit; mussels as biomonitors of water contamination; activity consistent with water concentration × bioconcentration factor ~100-200
notes: Mussels are standard radionuclide biomonitors (OSPAR HELCOM IAEA programs); Chernobyl Black Sea mussel data provides early 1987-1990 contamination record; declining consistently since 1990
source: Polikarpov GP 1992 J Environ Radioact; IAEA Marine Monitoring; Ukrainian Black Sea monitoring

context: Naturally elevated Po-210 (Ra-226 decay product) in Black Sea from upwelling of anoxic deep water; provides context for baseline natural radioactivity; adds to overall radiation dose from Black Sea seafood consumption; distinct from Chernobyl contribution
notes: Natural Po-210 in marine fish: 20-200 Bq/kg; dominates radiation dose from seafood consumption globally (natural >> anthropogenic); important context for Chernobyl contamination assessment
source: UNSCEAR 2000 Natural Sources; Hamilton EI 2002; food_agricultural_contamination_REAL.csv

context: Tritium (H-3; t1/2=12.32yr) from 1950s-1960s weapons testing elevated Black Sea surface water above oceanic baseline; by 1986 mostly decayed; not a Chernobyl-specific issue but part of baseline radioactivity context; Chernobyl released minimal additional H-3 (graphite activation product)
notes: H-3 from 1963 peak: ~1000 TU (tritium units) in precipitation worldwide; Black Sea surface water ~100-200 TU in 1966; declined to <10 TU by 1990s; entirely from weapons testing not Chernobyl
source: IAEA Tritium in the Environment; not Chernobyl-specific but baseline reference

context: Danube River catchment includes heavily contaminated areas of Central Europe (Hungary Romania Bulgaria Czech Republic Austria); total Danube Cs-137 input to Black Sea estimated 3-8 TBq 1986-2000; much less than Sr-90 due to same particle-reactive Cs-137 trapping in Danube reservoirs
notes: Danube has multiple reservoir dams that trap particle-reactive Cs-137 just as Kyiv Reservoir on Dnieper; far less Cs-137 reaches Black Sea via Danube proportionally; Sr-90 contribution ~60 TBq 1986-2000 (dnieper file)

context: Am-241 growing from Pu-241 decay (t1/2=14.35yr) in Black Sea sediments that received Pu-241 via fallout; particle-reactive like Cs-137; retained in near-shore sediments; total Black Sea Am-241 inventory still increasing and will peak ~2059; see am241_ingrowth_timeseries_REAL.csv for terrestrial CEZ analog
notes: Marine Am-241 ingrowth from Pu-241 is same Bateman equation process as in CEZ soils; less studied in marine context but same physics applies; adds to long-term radiotoxicity of Black Sea sediments
source: am241_ingrowth_timeseries_REAL.csv; Povinec 2004; IAEA Marine Env Lab
